Abstract

Translated from Chinese

一种包括混合电池组的车辆，该车辆包括第一电池组和第二电池组。第一电池组比第二电池组具有更高的能量密度。第二电池组比第一电池组具有更高的功率密度。功率逆变器模块连接在混合电池组和连接到车辆动力系的电动发电机单元(MGU)之间。功率逆变器模块被配置为调节混合电池组和MGU之间的功率流。电池管理模块被配置为：控制功率逆变器模块的切换；选择性地对第一电池组和第二电池组中的至少一个充电和放电；以及利用来自第二电池组的电力选择性地对第一电池组充电。

A vehicle including a hybrid battery pack includes a first battery pack and a second battery pack. The first battery pack has a higher energy density than the second battery pack. The second battery pack has a higher power density than the first battery pack. The power inverter module is connected between the hybrid battery pack and a motor generator unit (MGU) connected to the vehicle powertrain. The power inverter module is configured to regulate power flow between the hybrid battery pack and the MGU. The battery management module is configured to: control switching of the power inverter module; selectively charge and discharge at least one of the first battery pack and the second battery pack; and selectively charge the battery pack with power from the second battery pack. The first battery pack is charged.

Description

Energy sharing system and method for vehicle
Introduction to
The information provided in this section is intended to generally introduce the background of the disclosure. Work of the presently named inventors, to the extent it is described in this section, as well as aspects of the description that may not otherwise qualify as prior art at the time of filing, are neither expressly nor impliedly admitted as prior art against the present disclosure.
The present disclosure relates to energy sharing systems and methods for hybrid battery packs, and more particularly, to managing power flow from a hybrid battery pack based on a state of charge of the battery pack.
The powertrain transfers torque from one or more torque-generative devices to the driveline through the transmission. The torque-generative devices may include an internal combustion engine and a Motor Generator Unit (MGU).
A hybrid vehicle may include an internal combustion engine and one or more MGUs. An electric vehicle may include one or more MGUs, but no internal combustion engine. Other types of vehicles may include an internal combustion engine without including an MGU.
The MGU may operate as an electric machine to generate a torque input to the transmission independent of a torque input from the internal combustion engine. The MGU may also operate as a generator, converting vehicle kinetic energy into electrical energy that may be stored in a battery pack. The battery management module regulates power flow between the charging station, the battery pack, the MGU, and the accessory load.
Disclosure of Invention
In one feature, a vehicle is described. The vehicle includes a hybrid battery pack including a first battery pack and a second battery pack. The first battery pack has a higher energy density than the second battery pack. The second battery pack has a higher power density than the first battery pack. The power inverter module is connected between a hybrid battery pack and a Motor Generator Unit (MGU) connected to a vehicle powertrain. The power inverter module is configured to regulate power flow between the hybrid battery pack and the MGU. The battery management module is configured to: controlling switching of the power inverter modules; selectively charging and discharging at least one of the first battery pack and the second battery pack; and selectively charging the first battery pack with power from the second battery pack.
In further features, the vehicle further comprises a first switch and a second switch. A first switch is connected between the power inverter module and the second battery pack and (i) when open, disconnects the second battery pack from at least one of the power inverter module and the charging station; and (ii) when closed, connecting the second battery pack with at least one of the power inverter module and the charging station. A second switch is connected between the power inverter module and the first battery pack and (i) when open, disconnects the first battery pack from at least one of the power inverter module and the charging station; and (ii) when closed, connecting the first battery pack with at least one of the power inverter module and the charging station.
In further features, the battery management module is further configured to: determining a first state of charge (SOC) of a first battery pack; and determining a second SOC for the second battery pack.
In further features, the battery management module is configured to charge and discharge at least one of the first battery pack and the second battery pack based on at least one of the first SOC and the second SOC.
In further features, the battery management module is configured to discharge the second battery pack if: (i) while the vehicle is in a drive mode; (ii) When the second SOC of the second battery pack is greater than the first predetermined SOC; and (iii) when the first SOC of the first battery pack is less than a second predetermined SOC; and the battery management module is configured to charge the first battery pack with power discharged from the second battery pack if: (i) while the vehicle is in a drive mode; (ii) When the second SOC of the second battery pack is greater than a third predetermined SOC; and (iii) when the first SOC of the first battery pack is greater than the fourth predetermined SOC;
in further features, the battery management module is configured to discharge the first battery pack in response to determining that a second SOC of the second battery pack is less than a first predetermined SOC.
In further features, the battery management module is configured to determine whether the vehicle is plugged into a charging station; and the battery management module is configured to determine the level of the charging station in response to determining that the vehicle is plugged into the charging station.
In further features, the battery management module is configured to determine whether the first SOC of the first battery pack is less than a first predetermined SOC of the first battery pack in response to determining that the charging station is a three-level charging station; the battery management module is configured to charge at least one of the second battery pack and the first battery pack with power from a charging station in response to determining that the first SOC of the first battery pack is less than the first predetermined SOC of the first battery pack; and the battery management module is configured to charge the second battery pack with power from the charging station in response to determining that the first SOC of the first battery pack is greater than the first predetermined SOC of the first battery pack.
In further features, the battery management module is configured to determine whether the first SOC of the first battery pack is less than a second predetermined SOC of the first battery pack in response to determining that the charging station is not a three-level charging station, wherein the second predetermined SOC is greater than the first predetermined SOC; the battery management module is configured to charge the first battery pack with power from the charging station in response to determining that the first SOC of the first battery pack is less than the second predetermined SOC of the first battery pack; and the battery management module is configured to charge the second battery pack in response to determining that the first SOC of the first battery pack is greater than or equal to a second predetermined SOC of the first battery pack.
In further features, the battery management module is configured to determine whether the second SOC of the second battery pack is greater than the first predetermined SOC of the second battery pack and whether the first SOC of the first battery pack is less than the second predetermined SOC of the first battery pack in response to determining that the vehicle is not inserted into the charging station; and the battery management module is configured to, in response to determining at least one of (a) the second SOC of the second battery pack is less than the first predetermined SOC of the second battery pack and (b) the first SOC of the first battery pack is greater than the second predetermined SOC of the first battery pack, (i) at least one of inhibit discharge of the second battery pack and (ii) inhibit discharge of the first battery pack.
In further features, the battery management module is configured to: in response to determining that the second SOC of the second battery pack is greater than the first predetermined SOC of the second battery pack and the first SOC of the first battery pack is less than the second predetermined SOC of the first battery pack, determining whether an energy request has been received; and in response to determining that the energy request has been received, at least one of: (i) Enable charging of the first battery pack with power from the second battery pack, and (ii) selectively discharge the second battery pack to satisfy the energy request.
In further features, an energy sharing system is described. The energy sharing system includes a second vehicle including a battery pack and a second battery management module, at least one of: the second battery management module is configured to selectively charge the battery pack using power received from a hybrid battery pack of the vehicle; and the battery management module is configured to selectively charge the hybrid battery pack with power received from the battery pack of the second vehicle.
In further features, the energy sharing system further comprises: a first computing device associated with a vehicle and configured to transmit, in response to receiving a first input from a user, an energy request and a first location of the vehicle; the second computing device is associated with a second vehicle and is configured to: transmitting a second location of a second vehicle; and the amount of energy that can be sold from the battery pack of the second vehicle.
In further features, the energy sharing system further comprises an energy sharing server. The energy-sharing server is configured to: receiving a request for energy from a battery pack of a second vehicle, a first location of the vehicle, a second location of the second vehicle, and an amount of energy available for sale; in response to receiving the energy request, generating a list of energy vendor vehicles; and transmitting the list to the first computing device. The first computing device is configured to: displaying the list on a display of the first computing device; and in response to receiving at the first computing device a user input indicating a selection of a second vehicle from the list, sending an indication of the selection of the second vehicle to the energy-sharing server. The battery management module is configured to selectively charge the hybrid battery pack with power received from the battery pack of the second vehicle in response to a signal from the energy sharing server.
In further features, the energy sharing server is configured to limit the list of energy vendor vehicles to energy vendor vehicles within a predetermined distance of the vehicle location.
In further features, the energy request includes a location of the vehicle and a predetermined distance, wherein the first computing device is configured to adjust the predetermined distance based on a user input to the first computing device.
In further features, the second vehicle includes a charging port; the charging port controls access to the battery pack and includes an electronic lock; responsive to the selection of the second vehicle indicating in response to receiving at the first computing device a user input indicating a selection of the second vehicle from the list, the energy sharing server selectively transmitting an electronic access key to the first computing device in response to the indication of the selection of the second vehicle; and the electronic lock is unlocked in response to the electronic access key.
In further features, the electronic access key includes an amount of energy to be transferred from the second battery pack, and the battery management module is configured to charge the hybrid battery pack with power received from the battery pack of the second vehicle until the amount of energy transferred from the battery pack equals the amount of energy to be transferred from the battery pack.
In further features, the electronic access key comprises a predetermined time for which the electronic access key is valid. The battery management module is configured to charge the hybrid battery pack with power received from the battery pack of the second vehicle only when the current time is between predetermined times.
In one feature, a method for a vehicle includes: power flow between the hybrid battery pack and a Motor Generator Unit (MGU) is regulated by a power inverter module. The hybrid battery pack includes a first battery pack having a higher energy density than a second battery pack, and the second battery pack having a higher power density than the first battery pack. The method further comprises the following steps: controlling switching of the power inverter modules; selectively charging and discharging at least one of the first battery pack and the second battery pack; and selectively charging the first battery pack with power from the second battery pack.
Further areas of applicability of the present disclosure will become apparent from the detailed description, claims, and drawings. The detailed description and specific examples are intended for purposes of illustration only and are not intended to limit the scope of the present disclosure.

Detailed Description
Hybrid or electric vehicles may be propelled by an MGU that is powered by a battery pack. The battery pack may be configured to charge and discharge quickly (high power battery pack), or less quickly (high energy battery pack), but provide a longer range per unit volume or weight.
The hybrid battery pack includes a high power battery pack and a high energy battery pack so that the vehicle can have one battery pack that is rapidly charged and discharged and has a longer mileage. The battery management module manages vehicle power requests, prioritizing the vehicle power requests based on a state of charge (SOC) of the high power battery pack and a state of charge (SOC) of the high energy battery pack.
Referring now to FIG. 1, a functional block diagram of an example vehicle system is presented. While a hybrid vehicle system is shown and will be described, the present disclosure is also applicable to non-hybrid vehicles, electric vehicles, fuel cell vehicles, and other types of vehicles that include one or more MGUs.
The engine 102 combusts an air/fuel mixture to produce drive torque. An Engine Control Module (ECM) 106 controls operation of the engine 102. For example, the ECM106 may control actuation of engine actuators, such as a throttle valve, one or more spark plugs, one or more fuel injectors, valve actuators, camshaft phasers, an Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) valve, one or more boost devices, and other suitable engine actuators. The ECM106 may also control one or more other motors, such as a motor that can switch a water pump and an electric oil pump.
The engine 102 may output torque to the transmission 110. A Transmission Control Module (TCM) 114 controls operation of the transmission 110. For example only, the TCM114 may control gear selection within the transmission 110 and one or more torque transmitting devices (e.g., a torque converter, one or more clutches, etc.) within the transmission 110.
The vehicle may include one or more electric motors or motor-generator units (MGUs). For example only, the MGU122 may be implemented within the transmission 110, as in the example of FIG. 1. At a given time, the MGU122 may act as a generator or a motor. When acting as a generator, the MGU122 converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. The electrical energy may be used, for example, to charge the hybrid battery pack 144 and provide electrical energy to the electrical components of the vehicle. The battery management module 126 manages the charging and discharging of the hybrid battery pack 144. For example, the battery management module 126 controls power flow between the hybrid battery pack 144, the MGU122, and other loads 198. The battery management module 126 may also charge the hybrid battery pack 144 with power from the utility.
When acting as a motor, the MGU122 generates torque that may be used, for example, to supplement or replace the torque output by the engine 102. Although the MGU122 is shown and discussed as being within the transmission 110, one or more MGUs and/or motor-generator units external to the transmission 110 may additionally or alternatively be provided.
A Power Inverter Module (PIM) 134 may control the MGU122. In various implementations, the PIM134 may be referred to as a Transmit Power Inverter Module (TPIM) or a Traction Power Inverter Module (TPIM). The PIM134 converts DC power from the hybrid battery pack 144 to Alternating Current (AC). For example, the PIM module 134 may convert DC power from the hybrid battery pack 144 to three-phase alternating current power and apply the three-phase alternating current power to the windings of the MGU122. The PIM134 also converts AC power output by the MGU122, such as during regenerative braking, to DC power, and outputs the DC power to charge the hybrid battery pack 144. An Electronic Brake Control Module (EBCM) 150 may selectively control the brakes 154 of the vehicle. User interface component (UIM) 158 provides one or more driver inputs to Controller Area Network (CAN) bus 162. The CAN bus 162 may also be referred to as an automotive local area network bus. The control modules of the vehicle may communicate with each other via the CAN bus 162.
The driver inputs may include, for example, an Accelerator Pedal Position (APP) and one or more other suitable driver inputs. The Brake Pedal Position (BPP) may be provided to the EBCM150. Park, reverse, neutral, and drive rod (PRNDL) positions may be provided to the TCM114. In various embodiments, PRNDL locations may also be provided to PIM134. The ignition status may be provided to the body control module 180. For example only, the ignition status may be input by the driver via an ignition key, a button, a switch, or other suitable device.
An Accessory Power Module (APM) 196 provides power to an accessory load 198. The APM196 includes a DC/DC converter that converts power from the DC voltage of the hybrid battery pack 144 to one or more other DC voltages, such as 12 volts. By using the APM196, the accessory load 198 does not need to be redesigned to work with the higher voltage output of the hybrid battery pack 144.
The infotainment module 182 controls the content displayed on the display 184. In various implementations, the display 184 may be a touch screen display and signals indicative of user inputs to the display 184 are transmitted to the infotainment module 182. The infotainment module 182 may additionally or alternatively receive signals indicative of user input from one or more other user input devices 185 (e.g., one or more switches, buttons, knobs, etc.).
The communication module 194 includes one or more transceivers that wirelessly receive and transmit information via one or more antennas of the vehicle. Examples of transceivers include, for example, cellular transceivers, bluetooth transceivers, wiFi transceivers, satellite transceivers, and other types of transceivers.
The vehicle may include one or more additional control modules, not shown. One or more of the control modules may be omitted in various vehicles. The control module may selectively send and receive data over the CAN bus 162. In various embodiments, two or more control modules may communicate over one or more additional CAN buses (not shown).
Referring to fig. 2, the hybrid battery pack 144 includes a high power battery pack 204 and a high energy battery pack 206. The high-energy battery pack 206 has a relatively high energy density (i.e., energy per unit weight or unit size, e.g., in kilowatt-hours per kilogram (kWh/kg) or kilowatt-hours per liter (kWh/1)) relative to the high-power battery pack 204, thus extending the vehicle's range as compared to a battery system having the high-power battery pack 204 but not the high-energy battery pack 206. The high energy battery pack 206 may have a relatively high internal resistance, which limits its ability to charge and discharge as quickly as the high power battery pack 204. For example, the energy density of the high-energy battery pack 206 may be at least 50% greater than the energy density of the high-power battery pack 204.
In one embodiment, the high energy battery 206 includes lithium metal based energy cells having an energy density of 400Wh/kg, and the high power battery 204 includes lithium titanate based cells having an energy density of approximately 100 Wh/kg. In another embodiment, the high energy battery pack 206 includes lithium ion based energy cells having an energy density of 250Wh/kg and the high power battery pack 204 includes lithium ion based cells having an energy density of approximately 150 Wh/kg.
The high power battery pack 204 has a relatively high power density (i.e., power per unit size or per unit weight, such as kilowatts per kilogram or liters) relative to the high energy battery pack 206. For example, the power density of the high power battery pack 204 may be at least 100% greater than the power density of the high energy battery pack 206 using the allowable charge rate as a rough estimate of the power density of the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206, in one embodiment, the high power battery pack 204 includes battery cells that may be charged at 80% (SOC) at a 4C rate, and the high energy battery pack 206 includes battery cells that may typically be charged at about a C/3 rate. The 1C rate corresponds to the current required to charge the battery from a fully discharged state (0% charge) to a fully charged state (100% charge) in one hour. The 4C rate corresponds to the current required to charge the battery from a fully discharged state to a fully charged state in one quarter of an hour or 15 minutes.
High power battery pack 204 has the advantage of being able to accept higher currents during charging than high energy battery pack 206, enabling so-called "DC fast" or "three stage" charging. DC fast charging may be obtained from a charging source configured to provide a relatively high current, and may be, for example, a public charging station. As explained herein, access to such a charging source enables the vehicle to continue to drive off-set and provide faster partial or full charging of the high power battery pack 204.
The high power battery pack 204 is configured to provide a predetermined maximum range of the vehicle when fully charged and is capable of receiving a predetermined portion of charge equivalent to the maximum range during rapid charging (i.e., relatively high current charging) for a predetermined duration. For example, the high power battery pack 204 may be configured to provide a predetermined maximum range of 150 miles when fully charged, and be capable of receiving 80% of the range (i.e., 120 miles) during 15 minutes of rapid charging. Thus, if discharged from a fully charged state and then the high power battery pack 204 is rapidly charged to 80% of maximum SOC once, the high power battery pack 204 alone provides 270 miles of travel. Vehicle mileage is converted to kilowatt-hour battery capacity based on vehicle energy consumption per mile. For example, a vehicle may consume energy at a rate of 250 watt-hours per mile.
The high-energy battery pack 206 is configured to provide a predetermined maximum range in conjunction with the high-power battery pack 204. For example, hybrid battery pack 144 may be configured to provide a maximum driving range of 500 miles that is greater than or equal to the typical daily range of 75% of drivers on 361 days of the year.
The voltage ratings of the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206 may be the same or different. High power battery pack 204 and high energy battery pack 206 may have different end-of-charge voltages and/or different end-of-discharge voltages. To use the same PIM134 between the MGU122 and the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206, the voltage rating of the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206 may be between 250 and 500 volts (enabling the use of the same Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistor (IGBT)). For the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206, the end-of-discharge voltage should be above a predetermined fraction of the end-of-charge voltage, such as about 0.55 of the end-of-charge voltage.
The high power battery pack 204 includes a plurality of battery cells. The high-energy battery pack 206 also includes a plurality of battery cells. Each cell includes an anode and a cathode (shown in phantom on either side of the membrane). The one or more sensors of each battery cell 233 are in operable communication with each battery cell and are operably connected to the battery management module 126. The sensors 233 are configured to monitor battery parameters during vehicle operation. For example, the sensors 233 may monitor parameters indicative of the respective SOC of each battery cell, such as voltage, current, temperature, and the like.
Referring now to FIG. 3, a functional block diagram of an energy sharing system is shown. The on-board charging module 220 converts Alternating Current (AC) received from the charging station into Direct Current (DC) through an AC/DC converter and charges the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206. The onboard charging module 220 also detects when the vehicle is plugged into a charging station and what type of charging station the vehicle has been plugged into.
The first switch 254 is operatively connected to the high power battery pack 204 and the second switch 256 is operatively connected to the high energy battery pack 206. First switch 254 may also be referred to as a high power battery switch and second switch 256 may also be referred to as a high energy battery switch.
When the first switch 254 is open, the high power battery pack 204 is disconnected from the MGU122 and the onboard charging module 220. When the first switch 254 is closed, the high power battery pack 204 is operatively connected to the MGU122 (during the drive mode) and the on-board charging module 220 (during the charging mode). When the second switch 256 is open, the high-energy battery pack 206 is disconnected from the MGU122 and the on-board charging module 220. When the second switch 256 is closed, the high-energy battery pack 206 is operatively connected to the MGU122 (during the drive mode) and the on-board charging module 220 (during the charging mode).
In fig. 3, the first switch 254 and the second switch 256 are both shown in an open position. The battery management module 126 is operatively connected to each of the first switch 254 and the second switch 256, and is configured to control switching of the first switch 254 and the second switch 256 independently of each other. The first switch 254 and the second switch 256 may be placed in an open position, both the first switch 254 and the second switch 256 may be placed in a closed position, the first switch 254 may be placed in an open position and the second switch 256 may be placed in a closed position, or vice versa. High power battery pack 204 may be discharged without discharging high energy battery pack 206, and high energy battery pack 206 may be discharged without discharging high power battery pack 204.
The high power battery pack 204 may also be used to charge the high energy battery pack 206, and the high energy battery pack 206 may be used to charge the high power battery pack 204. For example, when high power battery pack 204 is powering MGU122 (i.e., first switch 254 is closed), second switch 256 may also be closed, such that high power battery pack 204 charges high energy battery pack 206.
Depending on the respective positions of the first switch 254 and the second switch 256, the MGU122 may be driven by power from the high power battery pack 204 and/or the high energy battery pack 206. Alternatively, depending on the respective positions of first switch 254 and second switch 256, the MGU may charge high power battery pack 204 and/or high energy battery pack 206. The MGU122 may be an Alternating Current (AC) motor or another suitable type of motor. The PIM134 is shown disposed between the MGU122 and the first and second switches 254, 256.
The energy management system may also include a third switch 258 for controlling current flow to the accessory power module 196 that powers the accessory load 198. The third switch 258 is operatively connected to the battery management module 126. The battery management module 126 controls the switching of the third switch 258. When the third switch 258 is in the closed position, current generated by the MGU122 during operation as a generator (during regenerative braking) is provided to an accessory load 198 on the vehicle, such as an electric vehicle accessory. During regenerative braking, the battery management module 126 may close the third switch 258, causing current to flow to the accessory load 198. This can be used to avoid high currents that damage the cells of the high energy battery.
Fig. 4 shows a functional block diagram of an example implementation of the battery management module 126. The battery management module 126 may include a state of charge (SOC) module 308, a battery sharing module 316, and a battery determination module 320. The SOC module 308 estimates the SOC of the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206 based on data from the sensors 233. The SOC module 308 may determine the SOC of the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206 based on the voltages of the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206. For example, SOC module 308 may determine SOC using one of a lookup table and an equation that relates the voltage of high power battery pack 204 and high energy battery pack 206 to SOC.
Additionally or alternatively, the SOC module 308 may determine the SOC based on the current to and from the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206. For example, the SOC module 308 may determine a mathematical integration of the current over each predetermined period and add the integration results to determine the SOC of the battery pack. As another example, SOC module 308 may scale or offset voltages based on current, an offset scalar determined based on current, and determine SOC using one of a lookup table and equations that relate these scaled or offset voltages to the SOC of high power battery pack 204 and high energy battery pack 206. SOC module 308 may further determine SOC based on the temperatures of high power battery pack 204 and high energy battery pack 206. For example, the temperature may be measured using one or more temperature sensors. The SOC may be provided as a percentage between 0% SOC representing 0 charge (i.e., fully discharged) and 100% SOC representing full charge of the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206.
The SOC module 308 includes a charger module 312. The charger module 312 monitors the SOC of each of the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206 and determines when the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206 are fully charged. The charger module 312 also charges the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206 in a manner that helps to extend the life of the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206. For example, during charging, when the high-energy battery pack 206 is fully charged, the charger module 312 instructs the battery determination module 320 to open the second switch 256 to prevent any more energy from flowing to the high-energy battery pack 206. Similarly, during charging, when the high power battery pack 204 is fully charged, the charger module 312 instructs the battery determination module 320 to open the first switch 254 to prevent any more energy from flowing to the high power battery pack 204.
The battery sharing module 316 enables energy sharing between vehicles, such as energy of a buyer vehicle (hereinafter "buyer") and energy of a seller vehicle (hereinafter "seller"). The battery sharing module 316 receives vehicle location data (geographical coordinates of the vehicle), SOC data for the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206, and transmits the vehicle location data and the SOC data to the energy sharing server. The battery sharing module 316 may periodically update and retransmit the SOC of the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206 of the vendor vehicle.
The battery sharing module 316 may also receive and transmit data, such as an energy access key, to the computing device. The energy access key controls access to the vendor vehicle charging port. The energy access key includes an amount of energy to be transferred and a time period for which the energy access key is valid. The charging port may include an electronic lock that may be locked and unlocked by the energy access key. For example, the buyer may establish a communication link between the buyer's computing device and the seller's vehicle using Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) communication. The purchaser may transmit the energy access key to the seller's vehicle using a BLE communication link. The vendor vehicle's CAN network 162 may wake up in response to receiving the energy access key and unlock the vehicle's charging port upon successful authentication of the energy access key. During the energy transfer transaction, battery share module 316 monitors the SOC of high power battery pack 204 and high energy battery pack 206 to determine when the amount of energy specified in the energy access key has been transferred to the purchaser's vehicle. The battery sharing module 316 instructs the battery determination module 320 to open the first switch 254 and/or the second switch 256 to prevent further energy transfer.
The battery determination module 320 selectively controls the discharging and charging of the high-power battery pack 204 and the high-energy battery pack 206 based on the SOC of the high-power battery pack 204 and the high-energy battery pack 206, a Vehicle Power Request (VPR), characteristics of a charging station, and an energy access key. The VPR includes the current amount of power required to meet the vehicle operator speed and acceleration commands. For example, depression or elevation of an accelerator pedal, rate of depression or elevation of a brake pedal, and wheel speed data may be used by the engine control module to determine VPR. For example, if the determined VPR is non-zero (i.e., the MGU122 is required as a motor), then power from the hybrid battery pack 144 is required. However, if VPR is zero, the MGU122 need not act as a motor.
The battery determination module 320 selectively controls the discharging and charging of the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206 by opening and closing the first switch 254 and the second switch 256, respectively. For example, in response to the SOC of the high power battery pack 204 being less than a predetermined minimum threshold, the battery determination module 320 may open the first switch 254 such that no more power is allowed to flow from the high power battery pack 204 and close the second switch 256 such that any additional VPR requests are satisfied by the high energy battery pack 206.
The battery determination module 320 selectively enables charging of the high energy battery pack 206 by the high power battery pack 204. For example, when the vehicle is in the drive mode, the SOC of the high energy battery pack 206 is greater than a first predetermined minimum threshold, e.g., 0%, and the SOC of the high energy battery pack 206 is less than a second predetermined minimum threshold, e.g., 80%, the battery determination module 320 closes the first switch 254 and the second switch 256. The vehicle may be in a drive mode when the vehicle is propelling the vehicle with energy from the hybrid battery pack 144.
FIG. 5 is a functional block diagram of an example energy sharing system. The energy sharing server 401 facilitates the sale of energy between vehicles. The buyer sends an energy request to the energy sharing server 401 using a computing device, such as computing device 402. Examples of computing devices include mobile phones, tablet devices, laptop computers, desktop computers, and other types of computing devices. The computing devices 402 and 403 and the energy sharing server 401 communicate via one or more networks 408 and 409. Networks 408 and 409 may include wireless networks, wired networks, or a combination of wireless and wired networks. While an example is provided in which a buyer submits an energy request via the computing device 402, in some implementations, the buyer may submit the energy request directly via the infotainment module 182 of the vehicle. In this manner, the infotainment module 182 of the vehicle is considered a computing device.
The energy request may include the location (e.g., geographic coordinates) of the buyer, the amount of energy requested to be purchased by the buyer, the distance the buyer is willing to travel to purchase energy, the current remaining mileage based on the SOC of the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206, and the maximum price the buyer is willing to pay for each energy metering unit, and other suitable information.
The seller sends the energy information to the energy-sharing server 401 through the computing device 403. The energy information may include: location of the seller (e.g., geographic coordinates), how much energy the seller has available for sale, the lowest price the seller is willing to sell energy per unit, the estimated mileage remaining for the vehicle based on the SOC of the seller's vehicle's high-power battery pack 204 and high-energy battery pack 206, and the time frame in which the seller is willing to sell energy. The seller may manually input the amount of energy available for sale, or the energy may be periodically updated based on the SOC of the seller vehicle's high power battery pack 204 and high energy battery pack 206.
Based on the energy request, the energy sharing server 401 determines a list of potential sellers that meet the criteria contained in the energy request. For example, the energy sharing server 401 may include in the list of potential sellers all vehicles within a distance that the buyer is willing to travel that have the requested amount of available energy and that are willing to sell energy at less than the highest price the buyer is willing to pay for each energy metering unit.
In response to receiving the list of potential sellers, the buyer can select one of the sellers from the list. The buyer sends the seller selected from the list of potential sellers to the energy sharing server 401. In response to the buyer's selection, the energy sharing server 401 sends a transaction confirmation notification to the seller confirming the details of the transaction, such as the amount of energy to be transferred, the price at which the buyer has agreed to purchase the energy, and the location (if different from the location of the seller) at which the transfer is to be made. Upon receiving the transaction confirmation, the seller transmits the energy access key to the energy sharing server 401, and the energy sharing server 401 then transmits the energy access key to the buyer. The buyer may then use the energy access key to unlock the charging port of the seller vehicle and charge the buyer vehicle with the requested amount of energy from the seller vehicle. Although the example provided is a purchaser vehicle equipped with a hybrid battery pack of the present disclosure, the purchaser vehicle may be equipped with any suitable battery pack, such as a high power only battery pack or a high energy only battery pack.
Fig. 6 includes a front view of an example implementation of a computing device 402. Fig. 7 includes a functional block diagram of an example implementation of a computing device 402. Referring now to fig. 6 and 7, the computing device 402 includes a Central Processing Unit (CPU) or processor 450, one or more input devices 454 (e.g., a touch screen display, a microphone, one or more switches, etc.), a display 458 (e.g., a touch screen display), one or more other output devices (not shown), a network interface 462, and memory 466. Although the input device 454 and the display 458 are shown as components of the computing device 402, the input device and the output device (e.g., display) may be peripheral devices. Further, although an example of a single processor is provided, computing device 402 may include two or more processors.
Network interface 462 connects computing device 402 to network 408. For example, the network interface 462 may include a wired interface (e.g., an ethernet interface) and/or a wireless interface (e.g., wi-Fi, bluetooth, near Field Communication (NFC), or other wireless interface). The processor 450 of the computing device 402 executes an Operating System (OS) 472 and one or more other applications. The processor 450 executes an Operating System (OS) 472 and one or more server applications, such as an energy sharing application 474, to display a user interface for generating and sending energy requests. The operations discussed herein as being performed by the computing device 402 are performed by the computing device 402. Although computing device 402 is depicted in fig. 6 and 7, computing device 403 may be similarly configured.
Fig. 8 includes a simplified functional block diagram of an example implementation of the energy-sharing server 401. The energy sharing server 401 includes a processor 504, one or more input devices 508 (e.g., keyboard, touchpad, mouse, etc.), a display subsystem 512 including a display 516, a network interface 520, a memory 524, and a mass storage 528. Although the input device 508 and the display 516 are shown as components of the energy sharing server 401, the input device and the output device (e.g., the display) may be peripheral devices. Further, although a single processor example is provided, the energy-sharing server 401 may include two or more processors.
The network interface 520 connects the energy sharing server 401 to the computing devices 402 and 403 through the networks 408 and 409. For example, the network interface 520 may include a wired interface (e.g., an ethernet interface) and/or a wireless interface (e.g., wi-Fi, bluetooth, near Field Communication (NFC), or other wireless interface). The memory 524 may include volatile or non-volatile memory, cache memory, or other types of memory. The mass storage 528 may include flash memory, one or more hard drives, or other mass storage devices.
The processor 504 executes an Operating System (OS) 532 and one or more server applications, such as an energy sharing application 536. The mass memory 528 may store one or more databases 540, the databases 540 storing data structures used by the energy-sharing server 401 application to perform the functions described herein. The processor 504 executes the energy sharing application 536 to facilitate energy sharing between buyers and sellers. The operations discussed herein as being performed by the energy sharing server 401 are performed by the energy sharing server 401 (and more particularly, the processor 504) during execution of the energy sharing application 536. Although the functions described herein are performed by the energy sharing server 401, the functions of the energy sharing server 401 may be distributed among two or more servers.
Fig. 9-11 depict example control operations performed by the battery management module 126. In 704, control determines whether the vehicle is in a drive mode. If control determines that the vehicle is in drive mode, control continues at 705. If control determines that the vehicle is not in drive mode, control continues at 728.
Control receives (VPR) 705, and control continues with 706. At 706, control verifies that the VPR has been received and is greater than zero. If so, control continues at 707; otherwise, control returns to 705. At 707, control determines the SOC of the high power battery pack 204 and the high energy battery pack 206. At 708, control determines whether the SOC of the high power battery pack 204 is greater than a first predetermined SOC or a similar predetermined SOC. If so, control continues at 712; otherwise, control continues at 724. At 712, control determines whether the SOC of the high energy battery pack 206 is less than a second predetermined SOC, such as 80%. If so, control transfers to 720; otherwise, control continues at 716.
At 716, control closes the first switch 254 (if previously opened) and opens the second switch 256 (if previously closed) so that only the high power battery pack 204 is supplying power to the MGU122, and control may end. While an example of ending is provided, control shows a continuous control loop, and control may continue back at 704. At 720, control closes first switch 254 (if previously open) and closes second switch 256 (if previously open) so that high power battery pack 204 powers the MGU and also charges high energy battery pack 206, and control may end. At 724, control opens the first switch 254 (if previously closed) and closes the second switch 256 (if previously open) so that the high energy battery pack 206 powers the MGU122, and control may end.
At 728, control determines whether the vehicle is plugged into the charging station. If so, control continues at 732; otherwise, control continues at 764. In 732, control determines a charge level characteristic of the charging station. At 736, control determines whether the charging station is a three-level charging station (i.e., DC fast charge). If true, control continues with 740; otherwise, control continues at 752. In 740, control determines whether the SOC of high energy battery pack 206 is less than a third predetermined SOC of high energy battery pack 206. For example, the third predetermined SOC of high energy battery pack 206 may be set to 30% or another suitable percentage. If so, control continues with 744; otherwise, control continues at 748. At 744, control closes first switch 254 (if open) and second switch 256 (if open) to enable DC fast charging of high power battery pack 204 and high energy battery pack 206, and control may end. At 748, control closes the first switch 254 (if open) and opens the second switch 256 (if closed) to enable DC fast charging of only the high power battery 204.
At 752, control determines whether the SOC of the high-energy battery pack 206 is less than a fourth predetermined SOC of the high-energy battery pack 206. The fourth predetermined SOC is greater than the third predetermined SOC. If so, control continues with 756; otherwise, control continues with 760. At 756, control opens the first switch 254 (if closed) and closes the second switch 256 (if open) such that the high energy battery pack 206 is charged before the high power battery pack 204, and control may end. At 760, control closes the first switch 254 (if open) and opens the second switch 256 (if closed) such that the high power battery pack 204 is charged first, and control may end.
At 764, control determines whether the SOC of the high power battery 204 is greater than a fifth predetermined SOC of the high power battery 204. If so, control continues at 768; otherwise, control continues at 776. At 768, control determines whether the SOC of the high-energy battery pack 206 is less than a fourth predetermined SOC of the high-energy battery pack 206. If so, control continues at 778; otherwise, control continues at 776. At 776, control opens the first switch 254 (if closed) and opens the second switch 256 (if closed). At 778, control determines whether an energy request has been received. If so, control continues with 782; otherwise, control continues at 780. At 780, control closes the first switch (if open) and closes the second switch (if open) to allow the high energy battery pack 206 to be replaced with the high power battery pack 204. At 782, control determines whether the seller has agreed to energy sharing (i.e., whether the seller has previously approved energy request sales). If so, control continues at letter A of FIG. 10, otherwise, control continues at 780.
Referring to FIG. 10, control sends an energy request to the energy-sharing server 401 at 808, and control continues at 812. At 812, the energy sharing server 401 receives the energy request, and control continues at 816. At 816, the energy sharing server 401 identifies a list of sellers based on the amount of energy requested and the location of the buyer. Control sends the list of potential sellers to the buyer at 820, and control continues at 824.
At 824, control determines whether the buyer has selected a seller from the list of potential sellers. If so, control continues with 828; otherwise, control waits for the buyer to select the seller. At 828, the buyer's selection is transmitted to the energy sharing server 401 and control continues at 832. At 832, control determines whether the seller has previously approved the energy sale. If so, control continues with 852; otherwise, control continues at 836. At 836, control sends the energy request to the seller for approval. Control continues at 840, where control determines whether the seller has approved the sale. If true, control continues at 844; otherwise, control continues at 848. At 844, control transmits the seller's approval to the energy sharing server 401. Control sends the seller's rejection to the energy sharing server 401 at 848 and continues at 864. At 864, the energy sharing server 401 updates the seller list and returns to 820.
Control continues at 852 where the energy sharing server 401 processes the energy transfer transaction and continues to 856. At 856, control sends a confirmation of the seller's approval to the buyer. Control continues to 860 where control sends the energy access key to the buyer through the energy sharing server 401 and control continues at letter C of fig. 11.
Referring to FIG. 11, at 904, control determines a position of the buyer vehicle relative to the seller vehicle. For example, the buyer vehicle may transmit the location of the buyer vehicle once every predetermined time. At 908, control determines whether a distance between the buyer vehicle and the seller vehicle is within a first predetermined range. If so, control continues at 912; otherwise, control returns to 904. At 912, control sends a location notification to the seller indicating that the buyer's vehicle is within a certain distance of the seller's vehicle. Control continues at 914, where control determines a second distance between the buyer vehicle and the seller vehicle. At 916, control determines whether the second distance is within a second predetermined range. If so, control continues at 920; otherwise, control returns to 916. At 920, control determines whether the buyer vehicle has stopped (i.e., the vehicle is stationary). If so, control continues at 924; otherwise, control returns to 920.
At 924, control pairs the buyer's computing device 402 to the seller vehicle using BLE communications and sends the energy access key to the seller vehicle. At 928, the vendor vehicle is awakened in response to receiving the energy access key. At 930, the computing device 403 sends an energy access key validation request to the energy sharing server 401. Control continues at 932 where the energy sharing server 401 verifies that the energy access key is still valid (i.e., the seller does not revoke access). If so, control continues at 936; otherwise, control may end. At 936, control determines whether the current time is within a predetermined time period specified by the energy access key. For example, the energy access key may be valid from 2: 00 to 5: 00 in the afternoon. If the current time is 8: 00 pm, the energy access key is no longer valid. If so, control continues at 940; otherwise, control may end.
At 940, control unlocks a charging port on the vendor vehicle. At 946, control closes the first switch 254 and opens the second switch 256 so that only the high power battery pack 204 transfers energy to the buyer vehicle. At 950, control establishes a connection between the buyer vehicle and the seller vehicle. For example, the purchaser may establish a direct connection with a charging port on the seller vehicle using a bi-directional charging connector. At 954, control verifies that the buyer vehicle and seller vehicle have established a connection. If so, control continues with 958; otherwise, control returns to 954. Control begins transferring energy at 958, and control continues with 962. At 962, control determines the amount of energy transferred. At 966, control determines whether the amount of energy transmitted satisfies the amount of energy specified in the energy access key. If so, control may end or continue to the letter D of FIG. 9; otherwise, control may return to 958.

Claims (9)

1. a vehicle, comprising:
a hybrid battery pack comprising a first battery pack and a second battery pack, wherein:
the first battery pack has a higher energy density than the second battery pack; and
the second battery pack has a higher power density than the first battery pack;
a power inverter module connected between the hybrid battery pack and a motor-generator unit connected to a powertrain of the vehicle and configured to regulate power flow between the hybrid battery pack and the motor-generator unit;
a battery management module configured to:
controlling switching of the power inverter module;
selectively charging and discharging at least one of the first battery pack and the second battery pack; and
selectively charging the first battery pack with power from the second battery pack; a first switch connected between the power inverter module and the second battery pack, and:
(i) Disconnecting the second battery pack from at least one of the power inverter module and a charging station when open; and
(ii) When closed, connecting the second battery pack with at least one of the power inverter module and the charging station; and
a second switch connected between the power inverter module and the first battery pack, and:
(i) Disconnecting the first battery pack from at least one of the power inverter module and the charging station when open; and
(ii) When closed, connecting the first battery pack with at least one of the power inverter module and the charging station.
2. The vehicle of claim 1, wherein the battery management module is further configured to:
determining a first state of charge of the first battery pack; and
a second state of charge of the second battery pack is determined.
3. The vehicle of claim 2, wherein the battery management module is configured to charge and discharge at least one of the first battery pack and the second battery pack based on at least one of the first state of charge and the second state of charge.
4. The vehicle according to claim 3, wherein:
the battery management module is configured to discharge the second battery pack when: (i) when the vehicle is in a drive mode; (ii) The second state of charge of the second battery pack is greater than a first predetermined state of charge; and (iii) the first state of charge of the first battery pack is less than a second predetermined state of charge; and
the battery management module is configured to charge the first battery pack with power discharged from the second battery pack if: (i) when the vehicle is in a drive mode; (ii) The second state of charge of the second battery pack is greater than a third predetermined state of charge; and (iii) the first state of charge of the first battery pack is greater than a fourth predetermined state of charge.
5. The vehicle of claim 4, wherein the battery management module is configured to discharge the first battery pack in response to determining that the second state of charge of the second battery pack is less than the first predetermined state of charge.
6. An energy sharing system, comprising:
the vehicle of claim 5;
a second vehicle including a battery pack and a second battery management module,
at least one of which:
the second battery management module is configured to selectively charge the battery pack using power received from the hybrid battery pack of the vehicle; and
the battery management module is configured to selectively charge the hybrid battery pack with power received from the battery pack of the second vehicle.
7. The energy sharing system of claim 6 further comprising:
a first computing device associated with the vehicle and configured to: in response to receiving a first input from a user, transmitting an energy request and a first location of the vehicle;
a second computing device associated with the second vehicle and configured to:
transmitting a second location of the second vehicle; and
an amount of energy that can be sold from the battery pack of the second vehicle.
8. The energy sharing system of claim 7 further comprising an energy sharing server configured to:
receiving the energy request, the first location of the vehicle, the second location of the second vehicle, and an amount of energy available for sale from the battery pack of the second vehicle;
in response to receiving the energy request, generating a list of energy vendor vehicles; and
transmitting the list to the first computing device,
wherein the first computing device is configured to:
displaying the list on a display of the first computing device; and
in response to receiving, at the first computing device, a user input indicating selection of the second vehicle from the list, sending an indication to the energy-sharing server to select the second vehicle; and
wherein the battery management module is configured to selectively charge the hybrid battery pack with power received from the battery pack of the second vehicle in response to a signal from the energy sharing server.
9. The energy sharing system of claim 8, wherein:
the second vehicle includes a charging port;
the charging port controls access to the battery pack and includes an electronic lock;
the energy sharing server selectively transmits an electronic access key to the first computing device in response to receiving a user input at the first computing device indicating selection of the second vehicle from the list, in response to the indication of selection of the second vehicle; and is
The electronic lock is unlocked in response to the electronic access key.
